newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan political fog remains despite party alliance.
newsitem.headline: Japan political fog remains despite party alliance.

text.p: The fog surrounding Japan's political future failed to lift on Thursday, despite a loose alliance cobbled together among Japan's biggest conservative party and its two former coalition partners.

The fresh alliance virtually ensures that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto can keep his job, but leaves unanswered the key questions of what his next term will achieve or how long it will last, analysts said.
On Thursday, Hashimoto, who heads the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), and leaders of the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party formally agreed on a package of policy goals.
The conservative LDP grabbed the biggest number of seats in an October 20 election for the 500-seat Lower House of parliament, but fell short of a majority by 12 seats.
That forced it to seek support from its former partners in the outgoing ruling bloc, but both the Social Democrats and Sakigake shied away from joining an LDP-led coalition cabinet.
Analysts said the fresh alliance would likely give an LDP minority government an added modicum of stability.

"The worst-case scenario of a minority government...that couldn't get the budget through and would have to resign next spring is probably avoided," said Jeff Young, who analyses Japanese politics for Salomon Brothers Asia.

Some said Hashimoto might keep his grip on power for as long as four years if he won added support from independents and defectors from the biggest opposition party, the Shinshinto (New Frontier Party). The Shinshinto is now in some disarray after winning only 156 seats in the election.

"Hashimoto has got time on his side," said John Neuffer, analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute. "The Socialists and Sakigake don't want an election, independents are angling to get back to the LDP, and the Shinshinto is in chaos."

But others cautioned that the policy pact was mostly a cosmetic touch-up for what would still be an LDP minority administration and that future disputes -- including those over security policies -- lurked.
An LDP official warned the future was uncertain. "Since we don't have a hostage (from the other parties) in the form of a cabinet member, this might not work at all," he said.
The new cabinet is expected to be formed after Hashimoto is formally voted in as prime minister on November 7.

The LDP administration's fate also hinges on the stance taken by the new reformist Democratic Party, which with 52 Lower House seats has decided to stay in opposition but cooperate on some policy issues, and on whether the Shinshinto succeeds in healing its wounds to act as a viable opposition, said Yasunori Sone, a political scientist at Keio University.

Precisely what the second Hashimoto administration will be willing or able to accomplish on key policies such administrative reform, deregulation and tax reform remains unclear despite the broad outlines of the policy platform.
Among the policy goals were reforms to curtail the power of the Finance Ministry, give more independence to the central bank and reduce the number of government ministries.

The parties' agreement specified the creation of a panel in parliament to discuss the tax system, including a revision of a controversial sales tax, but did not touch directly on a planned hike in that tax to five percent from three next April.
Economists expect the tax hike to be implemented but see some changes to ease the burden on consumers with low incomes.
Another new panel will review the conduct of bureaucrats, whose power over policy politicians say they want to curtail.
"There is a lot of scope for the parties to disagree on the minutiae of potential pieces of legislation," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers.
How hard Hashimoto will push for the deregulation is vital critics say, for future economic growth also remains in doubt.
Some businessmen and bureaucrats say Hashimoto is committed to freeing the economy of red tape and argue his close ties to bureaucrats make him just the man to achieve that goal, though slowly.
But others, including many foreign economists, say the measured pace of reform will likely be too slow.
"I think Japan will deregulate, but there is nothing here to tell me they will do it quickly, and in a way that will give maximum benefit to the economy," Jones said.
